summary: Captures requirements for adding IANA and RFC Editor processing state information to the IETF Datatracker, giving the community one place to follow a document from its first Internet-Draft version to publication as an RFC. It allows more automation between the groups involved.

eli5.summary: A package should be trackable from the sender to the post office to your door. This describes what is needed so one website can show a document's progress in every stage until it becomes an RFC.

questions: track document from draft to rfc
what are the iana states in the datatracker
how are iana and rfc editor states tracked
subtitle: Requirements for showing IANA and RFC Editor progress in the IETF Datatracker, from first draft to published RFC.

tldr.problem: The Datatracker, IANA and the RFC Editor run separate systems, so once a document is approved for publication the community cannot easily see where it stands.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists requirements for the Datatracker to show IANA review substates and IANA and RFC Editor queue states, and to exchange machine-readable data with both groups so manual steps can be automated.
tldr.outcome: The Datatracker would cover the life of an Internet-Draft from version -00 to RFC publication, while IANA and the RFC Editor keep ownership of their own states and data.

today: RFC 6359 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. It states that the state names it lists are defined by IANA and the RFC Editor and may change, so their live queues are definitive.

sections.title: Why Extend the Datatracker
sections.content:
The IETF Datatracker is a web-based system for managing information about Internet-Drafts and RFCs, IPR disclosures, liaison statements and other parts of the document process. It will be extended, under RFC 6174 and RFC 6322, to track a document from version -00 up to the request for IESG evaluation. After approval, however, the Datatracker, ICANN (performing the IANA function) and the RFC Editor run on separate systems with differing visibility. This document defines requirements so the Datatracker covers the whole path to RFC publication.

It does not define the IANA or RFC Editor processes. Each of those functions retains ownership of its own data, state names and tracking systems. Before approval, the Datatracker is the definitive source for IANA status. After approval, the IANA system is definitive and Datatracker data is only a reflection of it. The RFC Editor's system is always definitive for RFC Editor status.
sections.eli5: Three offices each keep their own notebook about a document. This asks the main website to copy their progress so everyone can see it, while each office stays the boss of its own notebook.

sections.title: IANA Information in the Datatracker
sections.content:
IANA reviews IETF stream documents at four points: IETF Last Call, IESG Review, Document Approval and RFC Publication. During Last Call the Datatracker should show five IANA substates: IANA Review Needed (the default), IANA OK -- Actions Needed, IANA OK -- No Actions Needed, IANA Not OK and Version Changed -- Review Needed. The last is set automatically when a new version appears, so IANA can check that its considerations have not changed.

If a document slated for an IESG telechat still shows IANA Not OK, Version Changed -- Review Needed or IANA Review Needed, it should be called out in the Agenda Package. Once a document is approved and enters the IANA queue, the Datatracker should display the IANA-defined state, record state changes in the History log, and be notified by IANA automatically. Appendix A lists the IANA states at the time of writing, but the live IANA queue is definitive.

The document also anticipates future support for expert reviews, and says IANA and the IETF Secretariat may change IANA state manually, intended only to correct issues.
sections.eli5: Each document gets a sticker such as 'not checked yet', 'checked and fine' or 'problem found'. The sticker changes automatically if the document is edited.

sections.title: RFC Editor Information in the Datatracker
sections.content:
Once a document is approved it enters the RFC Editor queue and is tracked with RFC-Editor-defined states. The Datatracker already shows some of this, but should add a History log line each time the state changes, and receive a machine-readable notification from the RFC Editor. The RFC Editor continues to provide a queue file for data extraction.

The Datatracker should add links to AUTH48 pages (which show which authors have approved the document) and to cluster pages (documents with normative reference dependencies or requested for simultaneous publication). When an RFC is published, the RFC Editor notifies the Datatracker, which records the RFC number and updates fields such as title, author list and page counts that may have changed during editing.

If a document is withdrawn, the responsible party, such as an AD or the Secretariat, should change its state to something other than RFC Ed Queue and record details in a text box. That change triggers an email to the RFC Editor and IANA so both remove it from their queues. Appendix B lists the RFC Editor states, including AUTH, AUTH48, EDIT, IANA, REF and MISSREF.
sections.eli5: When a document is in the final editing office, the website should show each step, link to the page where authors say 'yes, this looks right', and update itself when the final RFC comes out.

sections.title: Automation and Reporting
sections.content:
When a document is approved, the Datatracker should send the RFC Editor machine-readable data: the I-D string, title, author list with email addresses and organizations, expedited goal date, publication status, consensus (yes/no), source, IESG contact, document shepherd email and IANA actions required. Four of these fields need to be added to the Datatracker: Expedited Goal Date, Consensus, Document Shepherd email and IANA Actions Required. The Consensus field, as used in RFC 5741, determines the Status of This Memo text for IETF and IRTF documents.

For alternate streams (RFC 6322), the Datatracker should not expire I-Ds under review, should notify the approving body when a new version appears, and should list I-Ds in the Agenda Package by requesting stream. It should also let stream managers generate a uniform publication request.

A restricted Show Discrepancies feature, available to IANA, the RFC Editor and the Secretariat, would list records that look out of sync, and email interested parties at regular intervals such as weekly. One example is drafts with IANA state In Progress whose RFC Editor state is not IANA.
sections.eli5: Instead of people retyping the same details into three notebooks, the website would pass them along itself. A checker would also point out when the notebooks disagree.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document states that it does not propose any new Internet mechanisms and has no security implications for the Internet. It specifies requirements for a tool used by the IETF, IANA, the RFC Editor and the Secretariat, not a protocol on the wire.
sections.eli5: This is a wish list for a website, not a new way for computers to talk, so it does not add new risks to the internet.
